<reason>Side A (CON) won a close but clear debate on the verification-failure asymmetry. A's core frame—every leak in design law lands a child on a protected default account, while every leak in a ban lands a child on the full adult product with no legal protections—survived the whole exchange. B's best counter (B3.1: safe defaults don't stop contact-based harms like grooming) was answered squarely in A4 with contact rules (private-by-default, no stranger DMs) that were anchored in A's original opening, not invented late. A also repeatedly exploited a real tension in B's case: B claimed platforms are casinos that will degrade design rules, yet relied on those same platforms to run age checks; B's answer (one number vs infinite rule maintenance) was asserted but never resolved after A showed design rules are visible on the product surface and that B conceded fines force compliance. B's critical-mass argument was weakened by B's own concession that messaging stays open, which A used to show PRO exempted the sextortion vector. B's strongest surviving material was the cohort-norm shift and the "failure as exception vs architecture" framing, which kept the case competitive. Both sides answered pressure questions directly with proper A1/A2 format; both had minor clipping costs. A's progression, sharper comparison, and cleaner resolution of the decisive clash earn the win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B3.1 (safe defaults can't stop adult strangers from following and DMing a lying fourteen-year-old) versus A4.1–A4.2, where A extended private-by-default and contact rules to unverified accounts, arguing that under a ban the same lying child is fully discoverable because the law declares she doesn't exist. A's follow-through in the closing—"the law doesn't fail to notice her, it forbids noticing her"—crystallized the clash memorably.</best_rebuttal>
